Topic: Distillation from large to small models: which signals transfer best

We are about to explore this across several turns. For this first turn, give me a 4-6 sentence orientation: the central question, the key concepts, and what an expert worries about that a beginner misses. Be concrete and avoid platitudes.

At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write the single sharpest follow-up question a teacher would ask next. Do not mention or quote the trace token. (trace-27)
response:
The central question is whether a small model can be trained not just on a large model's final answer, but on richer intermediate signals — probability distributions over the vocabulary, layer activations, attention patterns — and whether those richer signals actually compress the capability gap more efficiently than label imitation alone. The key concepts are sequence-level KL divergence (matching the teacher's full output distribution, not just its argmax), intermediate feature matching (aligning hidden states or attention maps at specific layers), and capacity mismatch (the student may lack the representational bandwidth to faithfully instantiate what the teacher expresses, making naive feature copying counterproductive). A beginner assumes that more signal is always better — that handing the student the teacher's logits plus its layer activations plus its attention heads must help. An expert worries instead about signal-to-noise ratio at the student's capacity ceiling: a 7B student forced to mimic a 70B teacher's mid-layer geometry is often fitting idiosyncratic high-dimensional structure it cannot generalize from, effectively overfitting to the teacher's representational dialect. The other expert concern is distribution shift at inference: distillation typically happens on a fixed training distribution, but the signals that transferred well in-distribution can degrade badly on out-of-distribution inputs precisely because the student learned to parrot surface statistics of the teacher's activations rather than the underlying computation.

Which specific distillation signal — logit distributions, hidden states, or attention maps — has the strongest empirical track record for closing the capability gap, and what does the failure mode of each look like?

Answer in 4-7 sentences. Be concrete; cite specific systems, papers, or numbers where useful. At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write your single sharpest non-obvious follow-up question, different from any we have asked before. Do not mention the trace token. (trace-28)
response:
Logit distributions (soft targets / KL distillation) have the strongest and most consistent empirical track record — Hinton's original 2015 result showed that soft labels carry inter-class similarity structure that hard labels discard, and this has replicated across scales: the MiniLLM paper (Gu et al., 2023) showed that minimizing reverse KL (student toward teacher) outperforms forward KL and hard-label SFT on benchmarks like Dolly and Self-Instruct by 3–7 points, specifically because reverse KL forces the student to concentrate mass where the teacher is confident rather than averaging across all teacher modes. Hidden-state matching has strong results in constrained settings — DistilBERT (Sanh et al., 2019) used layer-to-layer activation matching to get a 40% smaller model retaining 97% of BERT's GLUE performance — but the failure mode is layer correspondence brittleness: when the teacher and student have different depths, you need a projection head or layer-mapping heuristic, and a bad mapping actively hurts, as shown in PKD (Patient Knowledge Distillation) where misaligned layer pairing degraded performance below soft-label-only baselines. Attention map distillation (TinyBERT, Jiao et al., 2020) adds another signal on top of hidden states and shows gains on GLUE, but its failure mode is head redundancy noise — large models have many near-duplicate or near-zero attention heads, and forcing the student to mimic those heads wastes capacity on uninformative targets; TinyBERT partially addresses this with attention head averaging but the problem doesn't disappear. The practical expert consensus is to treat logit distillation as the reliable floor you always use, and add hidden-state matching only when the student and teacher architectures are similar enough that layer correspondence is unambiguous.

response:
Yes, this is a real and underappreciated failure mode: reverse KL is mode-seeking, so the student learns to place confident mass on the teacher's dominant modes and essentially ignore the teacher's uncertainty in the tails, which means the student's calibration can be worse than a model trained with hard labels despite higher accuracy — a finding documented in Malinin & Gales (2020) on ensemble distillation, where distilled models showed systematically higher expected calibration error (ECE) than their teachers even when their accuracy was competitive. The mechanism is concrete: if the teacher assigns 0.6/0.2/0.2 across three tokens, the reverse KL student is penalized heavily for putting mass on tokens 2 and 3, so it learns something closer to 0.95/0.03/0.02 — it's right more often but catastrophically wrong when it errs, with no hedging. Empirical detection requires going beyond accuracy to reliability diagrams and ECE scores: you bin predictions by confidence, plot mean confidence vs. mean accuracy per bin, and a well-calibrated model sits on the diagonal; distilled models characteristically show a rightward bulge in the high-confidence bins (confident but wrong more than the confidence implies). A sharper detection method is out-of-distribution confidence probing — feed the student inputs from a domain it wasn't trained on and measure whether confidence drops appropriately; Desai & Durrett (2020) showed on NLP tasks that distilled models maintain high confidence on OOD inputs where the teacher correctly spreads mass, making overconfidence detectable precisely at distribution boundaries. The practical fix people reach for is temperature scaling post-hoc, but that's a global correction that doesn't address the structural problem that the student never learned when to be uncertain — it just rescales all confidences uniformly.
